atoms.sound: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia and flows through China for around 6,300 kilometres. It begins high in the Tanggoolah Mountains and ends in the East China Sea.

atoms.sound: The Korean Demilitarised Zone is a long buffer zone separating North and South Korea.

atoms.a: It is one of the world’s most heavily guarded and dangerous borders, with landmines, barbed wire and guards on both sides.
Visitors to the nearby Imjingak Park have tied millions of ribbons to the fence with messages of peace.
With little human activity for over 70 years, the DMZ has become an accidental nature reserve, with endangered species like red-crowned cranes.

hint.label: Tectonic plates
hint.text: Tectonic plates are huge pieces of the Earth’s surface that fit together like a giant jigsaw puzzle. They move very slowly and can cause earthquakes when they bump into or slide past each other.

atoms.b: Japan experiences thousands of earthquakes every ((++year second)) because it lies where four tectonic plates meet, and the movement of these plates causes the ground to shake.
atoms.sound: Japan experiences thousands of earthquakes every year because it lies where four-tectonic plates meet, and the movement of these plates causes the ground to shake.

atoms.b: As a result, Japan is well prepared against earthquakes. Many of its ((++buildings cars)) are designed to sway during strong shaking, which helps stop them from collapsing, and people regularly take part in earthquake drills.

The largest earthquake ever recorded in Japan was the Tohoku earthquake in 2011. It was so ((++powerful insignificant)) that it triggered a huge tsunami, which is a giant ocean wave caused by an earthquake.

atoms.text: Rice paddies are a defining feature of East Asia, and rice cultivation has shaped the region’s landscapes and local economies for thousands of years.
China grows more rice than any other country in the world. Its rice paddies produce over 200 million tonnes each year, making rice an important part of life for millions of people.
